question: Why do we split data into a training set and a test set?
good: So we can measure how well the model does on examples it never saw during training, which is how it will be used.
bad: Because that is how it is usually done.

question: What does a learning rate control?
good: How big a step the optimizer takes when it updates the weights after each batch.
bad: It controls how fast you learn things in class.

question: Why might a model score well on a benchmark but still be bad in practice?
good: The benchmark may not match real use, or its questions may have leaked into the training data, so a high score does not mean the skill transfers.
bad: Benchmarks are always right, so it cannot happen.

question: What is overfitting?
good: When a model memorizes its training data, including the noise, and does worse on new data as a result.
bad: When the model is too big to fit in memory.

question: Why is accuracy a poor metric on very imbalanced data?
good: A model that always predicts the majority class can score high accuracy while never finding the rare class you care about.
bad: Accuracy is always the best metric.

question: What does a tokenizer do?
good: It splits text into tokens, the units the model reads, and maps each one to an integer id.
bad: It counts how many words are in a sentence.

question: Why do we use a validation set?
good: To tune choices like hyperparameters on data that is not the test set, so the test score stays an honest estimate.
bad: To validate that the code runs.

question: What is the difference between precision and recall?
good: Precision is how many predicted positives are right; recall is how many real positives were found.
bad: They are the same thing with different names.
